options.a: Move the £1.5m overspend into the design contingency and revisit the frame at Stage 4
options.b: Quantify cost drivers and present options with cost/carbon/function trade-offs
options.c: Rebase the client budget to £18.5m and record the increase as a client change
options.d: Instruct the structural engineer to redesign the frame to the cheapest section sizes before costing

distractorExplanations.a: Absorbing a known overspend into contingency hides the variance and erodes cover for genuine unresolved risk; it is not value engineering.
distractorExplanations.c: Rebasing the budget without a client decision is not advice; the overspend must be diagnosed and options presented before any budget change.
distractorExplanations.d: Directing a redesign before quantifying cost drivers skips option appraisal; the QS advises on trade-offs rather than imposing specification cuts.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Level 3 design economics involves diagnosing overspends, facilitating VE, and revising elemental cost plans with documented rationale. Agreed adjustments are then carried into the updated cost plan.

options.a: An NRM2 bill of quantities measured in full to support the employer's agent's tender pricing
options.b: An NRM1 order-of-cost estimate using £/m² GIA rates for each building type and a single risk allowance on the total
options.c: An elemental cost plan with sub-element breakdown, quantified where possible, tied to the current design
options.d: An NRM3 life-cycle cost plan of maintenance and renewal costs over a 60-year period

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses NRM2 detailed measurement for works procurement with the NRM1 elemental cost plan required at RIBA Stage 3.
distractorExplanations.b: An order-of-cost estimate is the NRM1 deliverable for RIBA Stages 0–1; Stage 3 calls for a formal elemental cost plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses NRM3 maintenance and renewal cost planning with the NRM1 capital elemental cost plan requested at Stage 3.

options.a: The Stage 2 order-of-cost estimate uplifted by the latest BCIS all-in tender price index movement
options.b: A schedule of provisional sums and prime cost items reconciled to the client's original budget
options.c: A benchmark comparison of £/m² GIA against BCIS projects of similar type, location and size
options.d: Updated elemental cost plan with measured quantities where available, reconciled to previous stages

distractorExplanations.a: Indexing a Stage 2 estimate ignores two stages of design development; Stage 4 viability needs a measured cost plan reconciled to earlier stages.
distractorExplanations.b: Provisional sums and PC items cover undefined or nominated work only; they cannot demonstrate viability of the whole £45m scheme.
distractorExplanations.c: Benchmarking is a feasibility-stage check; at Stage 4 the design supports measured quantities reconciled to earlier estimates.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Stage 4 cost plans integrate measurement progress, design changes, and procurement strategy to confirm budget viability. Reconciliation should also reflect the tender strategy.

options.a: Build up target cost from supply chain input, risk register, and preliminaries
options.b: Set target cost at the employer's £28m budget and recover any shortfall through second-stage variations
options.c: Price preliminaries as a fixed percentage of the first-stage direct works estimate from the last framework job
options.d: Lock all subcontract prices at Stage 1 so second-stage tendering of packages is not needed

distractorExplanations.b: Adopting the employer's budget as target without a bottom-up build-up mis-prices risk, and planning to recover via variations is unsound commercial practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Preliminaries depend on this job's programme, site and method; a percentage borrowed from another call-off is not a substantiated build-up.
distractorExplanations.d: Two-stage D&B relies on competitive second-stage package tendering to firm up the target; locking prices at Stage 1 removes that market test.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Commercial management at Level 3 involves transparent target-cost build-ups and risk-aligned commercial structures. Agreed pain/gain mechanisms then set how any over- or under-run against target is shared.

options.a: Benchmark £/m² fit-out rates from BCIS for each route and choose the lower median figure
options.b: Whole-life implications, cost certainty, programme, design risk allocation, and tender price dispersion
options.c: The consultant fee saving under D&B versus the higher fee scale for a fully designed traditional route
options.d: Capital cost only, since cost certainty and design risk are fixed by the JCT form chosen later

distractorExplanations.a: BCIS £/m² medians do not capture differences in risk transfer, programme or cost certainty between procurement routes.
distractorExplanations.c: Fee comparison is one input only; route appraisal must weigh cost certainty, risk allocation, programme and tender price dispersion.
distractorExplanations.d: Cost certainty and design risk allocation are the main differences between routes, not something settled later by the contract form.

options.a: Apply the +4.2% BCIS movement once to the whole cost plan total and treat it as fixed until tender
options.b: Apply the general RPI rate rather than BCIS tender prices, since tender prices track retail inflation
options.c: Apply an evidence-based inflation allowance to relevant elements with stated basis
options.d: Leave inflation out and rely on the contractor's fluctuations clause under JCT Option C

distractorExplanations.a: +4.2% is past movement; with 14 months to tender a forward forecast of tender price inflation to the tender date is needed, not a one-off historic uplift.
distractorExplanations.b: Retail price inflation does not track construction tender prices; BCIS TPI or an equivalent construction index is the correct basis.
distractorExplanations.d: JCT fluctuations provisions operate post-contract and are often deleted; a pre-tender cost plan must still forecast inflation to the tender date.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Cost planners use BCIS or equivalent indices to project tender-time costs with documented assumptions. The allowance should be reviewed at the next stage as the tender date firms up.

options.a: Compare capital cost and construction programme only, as FM costs are budgeted by the estates team
options.b: Compare NRM1 elemental capital costs and BCIS benchmarks for each cladding system at Stage 2
options.c: Compare capital costs plus manufacturer-quoted maintenance intervals without discounting to present value
options.d: Compare capital cost, maintenance, replacement cycles, energy performance, and whole-life cost

distractorExplanations.a: Whole-life costing brings maintenance and replacement into the option decision; leaving them to the estates budget is not design economics advice.
distractorExplanations.b: This is a capital-cost comparison only; lifecycle advice also needs maintenance, replacement cycles and operating costs.
distractorExplanations.c: Whole-life cost needs verified data discounted to present value over an agreed period; undiscounted marketing intervals misstate lifecycle cost.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Level 3 design economics integrates capital and operational costs for informed option selection. The comparison should run over an agreed study period (NRM3 / BS ISO 15686-5).

options.a: Explain contingency covers unresolved design, scope, and market risk until tender
options.b: Reduce contingency to 2% because 80% design completion leaves only construction-phase risk
options.c: Transfer the contingency into the contractor's preliminaries so it is priced at tender
options.d: Explain that NRM1 fixes design contingency at 10% for every stage up to contract award

distractorExplanations.b: Design 'percent complete' is not risk retired; unresolved design, scope and market risk remain until tender and justify the allowance.
distractorExplanations.c: Employer design contingency is a client risk allowance; moving it into contractor preliminaries hides it and gives away the client's cover.
distractorExplanations.d: NRM1 does not prescribe a fixed percentage; risk allowances are assessed per project and should reduce as risks are resolved.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Design contingencies reflect residual uncertainty and should be managed transparently through stages. It should be reduced only as design maturity is evidenced.

options.a: Recommend the lowest return, as framework rates already fix scope and qualifications for all bidders
options.b: Analyse scope compliance, qualifications, preliminaries, risk, programme, and resource assumptions
options.c: Normalise the three returns to the mean and negotiate the highest bidder down to that figure
options.d: Rank returns on preliminaries percentage alone, since measured works rates are fixed by the framework

distractorExplanations.a: Framework rates do not neutralise tender qualifications or exclusions; a £1.7m spread signals scope differences that must be analysed.
distractorExplanations.c: Averaging and negotiating against a mean is not tender analysis; compliance, qualifications and risk pricing must be reviewed first.
distractorExplanations.d: Preliminaries are only one component; scope compliance, qualifications, programme and risk all drive the recommendation.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Commercial management includes rigorous tender return analysis beyond headline price. Only then should a recommendation be made.

options.a: Cost per workstation using a national BCIS office median, without a London location factor
options.b: Cost per m² NIA taken from net lettable rents in the area, converted at a standard yield
options.c: Cost per m² GIA or NIA using relevant BCIS benchmarks with adjustments for specification
options.d: Apply the 2,500 m² net area directly to BCIS £/m² GIA rates without a net-to-gross conversion

distractorExplanations.a: A national median without a London location adjustment understates central London costs; benchmarks need location and specification adjustment.
distractorExplanations.b: Rents and yields belong to development appraisal and valuation, not construction cost benchmarking for a budget estimate.
distractorExplanations.d: BCIS rates are per m² GIA; applying them to a net area without a net-to-gross adjustment understates the budget.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Feasibility budgeting uses appropriate functional units with transparent benchmark adjustments. Adjustments should also cover basements and site constraints.

options.a: Treat the enclosure as covered by the plant allowance, since NRM1 groups plant and enclosures in services
options.b: Cost the enclosure cladding only, as structural and services impacts are dealt with at Stage 4
options.c: Draw the enclosure cost from design contingency without reporting it as a change
options.d: Assess incremental cost of enclosure, structural support, access, and services diversions

distractorExplanations.a: NRM1 places roof plant enclosures and their structural support in other elements; the existing plant allowance does not cover them.
distractorExplanations.b: Associated structural support and services diversions are part of the incremental cost now, not a later-stage issue.
distractorExplanations.c: Contingency drawdowns should be reported against a priced change; silent use hides scope growth from the client.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Design economics requires incremental cost assessment of changes against baseline allowances. Only costs beyond the base plant allowance are new, but they are not 'free'.

options.a: Coordinated drawings, specifications, provisional quantities, and defined measurement rules
options.b: Stage 2 concept drawings and the outline specification used for the order-of-cost estimate
options.c: A priced NRM2 bill from a recent comparable project, re-indexed to current BCIS prices
options.d: The planning approval drawings and the client's room data sheets without engineering input

distractorExplanations.b: Stage 2 concept information supports an early cost plan, not a Stage 4 pre-tender estimate based on technical design.
distractorExplanations.c: Another project's bill may inform rates, but quantities must come from this project's coordinated Stage 4 design.
distractorExplanations.d: Planning drawings and room data lack the coordinated technical and services design a pre-tender estimate needs.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Pre-tender estimates at Stage 4 rely on coordinated design and stated measurement basis. Exclusions should be listed alongside.

options.a: Proceed to Stage 3 and resolve the £1.3m gap through value engineering after tender
options.b: Present options to align scope, specification, or phasing to the budget with quantified savings
options.c: Advise the client to raise the cost limit to £9.3m as the estimate reflects market rates
options.d: Restate the estimate excluding risk allowances and fees so it can be compared with the £8m limit

distractorExplanations.a: Deferring a known 16% gap to post-tender VE risks redesign and abortive cost; options should be presented at Stage 2.
distractorExplanations.c: Recommending a budget increase without exploring scope, specification or phasing options gives the client only one choice.
distractorExplanations.d: Stripping risk and fees to fit the limit misstates the cost; the comparison must be like-for-like with the cost limit.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: When estimates exceed budget, QS advice includes scoped options to close the gap. Residual risk for each option should be stated.

options.a: Apply overheads and profit to direct cost only, holding the £1.2m risk as an unpriced contingency
options.b: Add 9% to the £22m direct cost and absorb the £1.2m risk within the overheads percentage
options.c: Present a transparent build-up separating cost, risk, overheads, and profit
options.d: Set the price at the client's budget and back-calculate the profit margin from the difference

distractorExplanations.a: Risk is a real cost the contractor carries; leaving it unpriced erodes margin, so the selling price must include risk as well as OH&P.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding 6% and 3% as a flat 9% and hiding risk inside overheads obscures the build-up and under-prices the risk element.
distractorExplanations.d: Price-to-budget ignores the contractor's cost base; the selling price should be built up from cost, risk, overheads and profit.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Contractor commercial management uses structured price build-ups for governance and negotiation. Documented assumptions support negotiation.

options.a: Revised budget figure reflecting the overrun, with previous variances reset to zero
options.b: Contingency drawdown to absorb the 6% overrun, with an amber RAG status for the period
options.c: Elemental comparison to BCIS benchmarks showing the overrun is within market norms
options.d: Cause analysis, forecast final cost, mitigations, contingency status, and decisions required

distractorExplanations.a: Resetting variances breaks the audit trail; reports must show movement from the approved budget and its causes.
distractorExplanations.b: Contingency is not there to absorb a 6% overrun silently; the report must analyse cause and seek client decisions.
distractorExplanations.c: Benchmark comparison does not explain the variance against this client's approved budget or set out mitigations.

options.a: Split elemental cost plans by use with shared infrastructure apportioned on an agreed basis
options.b: One blended elemental cost plan with residential and commercial split by GIA percentage at the end
options.c: Separate cost plans by use, with all shared basement and podium costs charged to the commercial use
options.d: Separate cost plans by use, leaving shared cores and plant out as a landlord cost

distractorExplanations.b: A pro-rata GIA split after the fact ignores differing specifications per use; funders need use-specific elemental plans.
distractorExplanations.c: Shared infrastructure must be apportioned on an agreed basis, not loaded onto one use, or each funder's figure is distorted.
distractorExplanations.d: Shared cores and plant are real construction costs and must be apportioned, not dropped from both cost plans.

options.a: Pay the full £500k to the contractor as a bonus, as the share ratio applies to overruns but not savings
options.b: Apply the agreed share mechanism, document calculation, and adjust final payment
options.c: Retain the full saving for the client, as gain share is payable under NEC Option D but not Option C
options.d: Hold the gain share until the next framework call-off and set it against any future overrun

distractorExplanations.a: Treats pain/gain as overrun-only; the agreed 60:40 mechanism splits savings as well as overruns, so the £500k is shared.
distractorExplanations.c: Wrongly limits gain share to Option D; NEC Options C and D both carry a pain/gain mechanism, so the agreed share must be paid.
distractorExplanations.d: Gain share is a project-specific contractual payment; carrying it to another call-off without agreement breaches the contract terms.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Target-cost commercial management includes correct pain/gain administration. Payment follows the contract terms.

options.a: Compare capital cost for each frame and defer carbon reporting to Stage 4 for the BREEAM submission
options.b: Compare operational energy and capital cost, since the frame drives the building's energy use
options.c: Compare embodied carbon and capital cost for steel, concrete, and timber options
options.d: Compare embodied carbon, treating capital cost differences between frames as negligible at Stage 3

distractorExplanations.a: Frame choice locks in embodied carbon at Stage 3; deferring carbon to a Stage 4 BREEAM report removes it from the option appraisal.
distractorExplanations.b: Frame choice mainly drives embodied carbon; operational energy depends on envelope and services, not structural material.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops cost from integrated advice; capital cost differences between steel, concrete and timber frames are material and must be quantified.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Design economics now commonly integrates cost and embodied carbon in option appraisals. Whole-life implications should be stated alongside.

options.a: Reduce MEP rates to the 32% benchmark and carry the 6% difference as a design risk
options.b: Accept the 38% because benchmarks are only valid for order-of-cost estimates at Stage 1
options.c: Re-allocate builder's work in connection with services into substructure to normalise the ratio
options.d: Investigate drivers — plant complexity, sustainability targets, riser strategy — and report findings

distractorExplanations.a: Forcing rates to a benchmark ignores project-specific drivers; a variance needs investigation, not arbitrary adjustment.
distractorExplanations.b: Benchmarks remain a useful diagnostic at every stage; a six-point variance at Stage 3 must be investigated.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving BWIC out of services to hit a ratio misstates the NRM1 elemental split rather than explaining the variance.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Benchmark variance analysis is a key Level 3 cost planning diagnostic skill. Findings should state the normalisation basis used.

options.a: Tender-stage cost plan with defined scope, quantified provisional items, and stated residual risks
options.b: Fixed contract sum under JCT D&B, which transfers all variation risk to the contractor
options.c: Assurance that the lowest tender will match the cost plan within the design contingency
options.d: Certification that the contractor's proposals meet the ERs, fixing the final cost at Stage 4

distractorExplanations.b: A JCT D&B lump sum still moves with employer changes and relevant events; it does not remove variation risk from the employer.
distractorExplanations.c: Tender outcomes depend on market and bidder pricing; a QS cannot assure that tenders will fall within contingency.
distractorExplanations.d: Contractor's proposals arrive at tender and do not fix final cost; certainty depends on scope definition and residual risk.

options.a: Arithmetic errors in the priced schedule, as a 20% gap usually signals a pricing mistake rather than scope
options.b: Scope compliance, exclusions, programme, insurances, technical compliance, and financial standing
options.c: Whether the price can be used to negotiate the other three bidders down before award
options.d: Programme and resource levels, since large price gaps between subcontractors mainly reflect labour productivity

distractorExplanations.a: Arithmetic checks are part of review, but a 20% gap more often reflects exclusions or scope gaps that must be checked first.
distractorExplanations.c: Using a low quote to Dutch-auction other bidders is poor practice and skips the scope and capability review.
distractorExplanations.d: Attributes the gap to productivity; scope compliance, exclusions, insurances, technical and financial standing must be checked first.

options.a: How you priced the final NRM2 bill of quantities for tender, with rates built up from first principles
options.b: How the cost plan at each stage matched the client budget without any changes needed
options.c: How estimates progressed from order-of-cost to pre-tender with key design decisions and VE
options.d: How you managed the final account and agreed variations with the contractor after completion

distractorExplanations.a: NRM2 bill pricing shows measurement and pricing skill, not the Level 3 design-economics narrative of cost plan evolution.
distractorExplanations.b: Assessors look for how you advised on change and overspend; a no-change story shows no Level 3 reasoning.
distractorExplanations.d: Final account work belongs to post-contract competencies, not design economics and cost plan evolution.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: APC Level 3 design economics is demonstrated through staged cost plan evolution and advice. Market feedback on pricing strengthens the narrative.

options.a: Combined cost plan at current prices, with Phase 2 shown as an option to be priced later
options.b: Phase 2 shown as a £/m² order-of-cost estimate at today's prices, revisited when funded
options.c: Phase 2 priced at Phase 1 tender rates plus the 2% annual CPI target for three years
options.d: Separate cost plan with escalation assumptions and interface costs between phases

distractorExplanations.a: Phase 2 starts in three years; current prices without escalation understate its cost and mislead funding decisions.
distractorExplanations.b: A current-price order-of-cost misses escalation and phase interface costs that affect the overall budget.
distractorExplanations.c: CPI is not a construction tender price index; escalation should use BCIS or similar forecasts, plus interface costs.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Phased developments need stage-specific cost plans and interface cost allowances. Enabling works allowances for Phase 2 should also be included.

options.a: Include as separate cost groups with clear exclusion from building contract scope
options.b: Include the loose FF&E in the main contractor's lump sum so it falls under one contract
options.c: Exclude FF&E as an operator cost outside the QS remit, noting it in the assumptions schedule
options.d: Carry FF&E as a provisional sum inside the contractor's preliminaries for later instruction

distractorExplanations.b: Loose FF&E is usually procured separately by the operator; folding it into the building contract blurs scope and adds main contractor markup.
distractorExplanations.c: Total project cost advice should carry client-defined FF&E allowances; parking it in the assumptions understates the hotel budget.
distractorExplanations.d: Preliminaries cover site running costs; FF&E is not a preliminaries item and should be a separate cost group.

options.a: Quantify savings in external wall area only, since floor-to-floor height affects cladding quantities
options.b: Quantify savings in cladding, structure, and MEP against impacts on services capacity and net area
options.c: Apply a standard 3% saving per 100 mm reduction from BCIS and adjust the cost plan
options.d: Quantify structural savings and confirm the planning height limit, deferring MEP review to Stage 4

distractorExplanations.a: Height reduction also changes structure, risers and MEP distribution space; cladding alone understates the trade-off.
distractorExplanations.c: BCIS publishes no such standard factor; savings must be quantified for this building's elements and performance impacts.
distractorExplanations.d: Ceiling void and services capacity are the main risks of lower heights and must be assessed now, not deferred.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: VE on floor-to-floor height requires cross-discipline cost and performance trade-off analysis. Acoustic performance should also be checked.

options.a: Recommend award at once, as a compliant bid below cost plan confirms the estimate was prudent
options.b: Reject the bid as abnormally low under the Procurement Act once it is 10% below the cost plan
options.c: Review scope gaps, rates, programme, and qualifications; reconcile to cost plan
options.d: Revise the cost plan down to the tender figure and release the £410k to the client's contingency

distractorExplanations.a: Being compliant on submission does not confirm price sustainability; rates, scope gaps and qualifications need review first.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no fixed 10% abnormally-low threshold; the bidder must be asked to explain its price before any rejection.
distractorExplanations.d: Releasing savings before reconciling scope and rates risks hidden gaps; the tender must be scrutinised first.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Post-tender employer advice reconciles tenders to cost plans with compliance checks. Then advise on award or clarification.

options.a: Head office overheads and profit, apportioned on turnover across the 18-month programme
options.b: A £/m² preliminaries rate from BCIS for city-centre offices applied to the GIA
options.c: Design fees and statutory approvals, as these drive time-related preliminaries on rebuilds
options.d: Site logistics, hoarding, craneage, working hours restrictions, and phased possession

distractorExplanations.a: Head office OH&P is a separate pricing item; preliminaries are driven by site-specific logistics and time-related costs.
distractorExplanations.b: Benchmarked £/m² rates ignore programme length and site constraints; preliminaries need a time- and method-based build-up.
distractorExplanations.c: Design fees and approvals are project costs outside contractor's preliminaries; site logistics drive preliminaries cost.

options.a: Investigation allowances, remediation risk, temporary works, and programme differential
options.b: New build elemental rates from BCIS, with retention priced as a percentage of the new build cost
options.c: Embodied carbon savings of retention only, as cost is assumed to favour new build at feasibility
options.d: Demolition and enabling costs for new build, with retention costs taken from the 1960s drawings

distractorExplanations.b: A percentage-of-new-build allowance ignores the frame's condition, remediation and temporary works risks.
distractorExplanations.c: Carbon is a valid factor, but the cost appraisal still needs investigation, remediation and programme allowances.
distractorExplanations.d: Original drawings are unreliable for 1960s frames; intrusive investigation and remediation risk allowances are needed.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: New build vs retention appraisals need full lifecycle and risk-adjusted cost comparison. Operational disruption costs should also be included.

options.a: Current cost plan total against budget, with commentary limited to items over a 5% threshold
options.b: Budget status, design development impact, risk/contingency, forecast final cost, and actions for approval
options.c: Cash flow forecast and drawdown schedule, with the cost plan issued only at stage gateways
options.d: Committed costs to date and consultant fee invoices, reconciled against the funding agreement terms

distractorExplanations.a: A total-versus-budget figure omits forecast final cost, risk status and the decisions funders need to approve.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash flow is useful to funders, but quarterly reports must also track budget, design change impact and risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Committed costs are a post-contract measure; design-stage reports must forecast final cost and design change impact.

options.a: Hold the margin forecast at tender level until the final account is agreed, to avoid a write-down
options.b: Submit global claims for all delays to recover margin before reforecasting the cost to complete
options.c: Reforecast, identify recovery options, escalate commercially, and document margin mitigation
options.d: Cut remaining subcontract packages by 10% through post-award renegotiation to restore margin

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying recognition of a known loss breaches commercial governance; forecasts must reflect the current position.
distractorExplanations.b: Global claims without causation rarely succeed; reforecast first and pursue only substantiated entitlements.
distractorExplanations.d: Squeezing let subcontracts is unsound and damages the supply chain; recovery must be planned and escalated.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Commercial management includes honest forecasting and structured recovery on distressed jobs. Mitigation should be agreed with site and head office.

options.a: The quote excludes VAT; recommend restating the external works element gross of VAT for the client
options.b: External works should be a provisional sum until the landscape design is complete
options.c: Paving belongs in NRM1 substructure, so the element should be moved before review
options.d: Single-source pricing lacks competitive market test; recommend benchmark or tender comparison

distractorExplanations.a: Cost plans are normally reported net of VAT; the real weakness is that one vendor quote gives no market test.
distractorExplanations.b: Provisional sums suit undefined scope; designed paving should be priced, but from more than one source.
distractorExplanations.c: Paving sits in the NRM1 external works group, not substructure; element coding is not the pricing weakness here.

options.a: Cost plan scope and exclusions must mirror ERs, drawings, and stated provisional items
options.b: Cost plan should follow the contractor's proposals, since these take precedence over the ERs
options.c: Cost plan elements must be renamed to match the JCT D&B contract clauses before tender
options.d: Cost plan should mirror the JCT activity schedule format required under the D&B contract

distractorExplanations.b: Under JCT D&B the ERs set the employer's scope; the cost plan aligns to them and contractor's proposals do not override them.
distractorExplanations.c: Contract clauses govern administration, not cost plan structure; the key link is scope, exclusions and provisional items.
distractorExplanations.d: Activity schedules are an NEC Option A/C concept; JCT D&B uses a contract sum analysis, and scope alignment matters most.

options.a: A note of the BCIS steel price index trend over the last five years, appended to the cost plan
options.b: Elemental sensitivity on steel package with percentage and absolute impact on total cost
options.c: A single steel price uplift of 15% added to contingency, with no scenarios modelled
options.d: A recommendation to fix steel prices now through a JCT fluctuations Option A clause

distractorExplanations.a: Historic index trends describe past movement but do not quantify the impact of volatility on this tower's cost.
distractorExplanations.c: One uplift is not sensitivity analysis; it needs scenarios showing percentage and absolute impact on the total.
distractorExplanations.d: JCT fluctuations Option A covers contributions, levies and taxes only; it neither fixes steel prices nor quantifies sensitivity.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Design-stage sensitivity analysis quantifies material price risk on total project cost. Impact on funding headroom should be shown.

options.a: Lead with the most aggressive price, since the price envelope is opened before technical scores
options.b: Finalise the price envelope first and adapt the technical solution to fit the target price
options.c: Technical compliance first, then price submission with internal walk-away thresholds
options.d: Submit alternative technical bids in one envelope with prices, to maximise evaluation options

distractorExplanations.a: In two-envelope tenders technical scoring normally comes first, and non-compliant bids may never reach price opening.
distractorExplanations.b: Pricing before fixing the technical solution risks non-compliance and mispriced scope in a two-envelope process.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixing price with technical content breaches two-envelope rules and can invalidate the submission.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Two-envelope tender strategy balances technical compliance with disciplined commercial pricing. A risk review should support the price.

options.a: Provide an order-of-cost estimate instead, as NRM1 permits elemental plans only from Stage 3
options.b: Produce an NRM2 trade-based estimate from the massing model, then map it to elements later
options.c: Use a comparable project's elemental cost plan rebased by BCIS indices without design adjustment
options.d: Prepare elemental cost plan with assumptions per element and flag uncertainty

distractorExplanations.a: NRM1 formal cost plan 1 is produced at Stage 2; massing-led elemental plans are normal with stated assumptions.
distractorExplanations.b: NRM2 trade measurement needs detailed design; elemental cost planning at Stage 2 follows the NRM1 structure.
distractorExplanations.c: Comparable data is a start, but each element must be adjusted to this scheme's massing, specification and site.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Early elemental cost plans are assumption-led with clear uncertainty flags. Measurement should be planned for Stage 3.

options.a: Separate identifiable allowances for party wall, logistics, and restrictions within relevant elements
options.b: A single abnormal costs percentage on the total, based on BCIS city-centre adjustment factors
options.c: Party wall surveyor fees in professional fees, with physical works left to the contractor's risk
options.d: Abnormal costs carried within design contingency so the elemental rates stay comparable

distractorExplanations.b: A blanket BCIS location factor does not identify party wall or logistics costs for client decisions on this site.
distractorExplanations.c: Party wall awards often require physical works such as underpinning or monitoring, which must be allowed in the cost plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Hiding known abnormals in contingency erodes cover for genuine unknowns; they should be identified allowances.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Abnormal site costs should be explicitly allowed in cost plans with justification. Where not element-specific, they can sit in risk.

options.a: Hold the pre-tender elemental split and report the total, as the tender sum is now fixed
options.b: Rebalance forecast, confirm scope transfers with design team, and update post-tender cost plan/report
options.c: Net the fittings underspend against the MEP overrun and report a single net variance figure to the client
options.d: Instruct MEP omissions to bring the element back to its cost plan allowance before contract

distractorExplanations.a: The tender sum fixes price, not element allocations; the post-tender cost plan must reflect tender pricing per element.
distractorExplanations.c: Netting hides why elements moved; scope transfers between fittings and MEP must be confirmed with the design team and reported by element.
distractorExplanations.d: Omitting MEP scope to fit a budget ignores design requirements; rebalance the forecast across elements first.

options.a: Confidentiality only — a non-disclosure clause in each appointment resolves the overlap
options.b: No conflict, as the PQS remit ends once the employer's cost plan is issued at Stage 4
options.c: Conflict of interest — separate teams or declined appointment needed
options.d: Fee transparency — both fees must be disclosed to RICS before accepting the roles

distractorExplanations.a: An NDA addresses information leaks but not the conflict of acting for both employer and contractor on the same works.
distractorExplanations.b: The PQS normally continues into tender and post-contract; acting for the contractor on the same works is a conflict.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosing fees to RICS is not the issue; the dual role creates a conflict of interest needing barriers or refusal.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Independence in employer cost planning conflicts with contractor commercial pricing roles. This protects the client and market fairness.

options.a: Price Category A at shell and core rates, assuming tenant contributions will cover fit-out
options.b: Recommend Category B fit-out instead, as it sits between shell and core and Category A
options.c: Reduce the Category A specification to fit the budget and record the changes in the risk register
options.d: Define specification tiers with cost ranges and facilitate client choice against budget

distractorExplanations.a: Assuming tenant contributions without agreement understates cost; Category A carries a real premium over shell and core.
distractorExplanations.b: Category B is tenant-specific fit-out beyond Category A, not a cheaper tier between shell and core and Category A.
distractorExplanations.c: Specification downgrades need a client decision on priced options; recording them in the risk register is not consent.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Specification advice maps fit-out levels to cost with client-led decisions. Market evidence supports the cost ranges.

options.a: Model N+1 or 2N redundancy costs explicitly in MEP elements with basis of design stated
options.b: Apply BCIS office MEP rates uplifted by a standard data centre location factor
options.c: Carry redundancy as a percentage add-on in design contingency until the tier is chosen
options.d: Model redundancy in the NRM3 renewals plan, as backup plant is a lifecycle replacement item

distractorExplanations.b: Location factors adjust for region, not building type; data centre redundancy needs explicit MEP modelling.
distractorExplanations.c: Redundancy level is a core design parameter, not a risk; it must be modelled in MEP elements with its basis stated.
distractorExplanations.d: NRM3 covers maintenance and renewal; the capital cost of N+1 or 2N plant belongs in the NRM1 MEP elements.

options.a: Cost reimbursement with a fixed fee, as call-off scope is not known at framework award
options.b: Priced schedule of rates or bill of quantities with defined adjustment rules for scope changes
options.c: A single lump sum agreed at framework award covering the framework's future call-off packages
options.d: Daywork rates under the RICS definition of prime cost as the default basis for call-off works

distractorExplanations.a: Cost-reimbursable call-offs give little price certainty; frameworks normally fix rates with adjustment rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Call-off scope is unknown at framework award, so a lump sum for future call-off packages cannot be priced reliably.
distractorExplanations.d: Daywork is a fallback for work that cannot be valued otherwise; using it as the default removes price competition and certainty.

options.a: Add a fee allowance as a percentage of construction cost within preliminaries
options.b: Exclude consultant fees, as NRM1 limits the cost plan to the building works estimate only
options.c: Separate consultant and construction cost groups with clearly defined inclusion/exclusion boundaries
options.d: Include consultant fees within the main contractor's overheads and profit to report one figure

distractorExplanations.a: Consultant fees are a separate NRM1 project cost group, not part of contractor preliminaries.
distractorExplanations.b: NRM1 cost plans include project and design team fees as a separate group when the client asks for total project cost.
distractorExplanations.d: Contractor OH&P is a construction cost; merging consultant fees into it double-counts and obscures fee scope.

options.a: Compare pod unit prices from three suppliers, with traditional bathrooms priced from BCIS rates
options.b: Assess pods on embodied carbon and BREEAM credits, leaving cost comparison to the contractor at tender
options.c: Compare capital costs only, with crane hire and loading-bay logistics left in the contractor's preliminaries
options.d: Compare pod capital cost, programme saving, quality control, and logistics against traditional build

distractorExplanations.a: Supplier price comparison captures capital cost only; programme, quality and logistics drive the net benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: Sustainability is relevant, but the VE decision needs QS cost evidence on capital, programme and logistics now.
distractorExplanations.c: Cranage and logistics change with pods and must be counted in the net comparison, not left as unpriced preliminaries.

options.a: Change reference, elemental impact, comparison to allowance, and updated forecast
options.b: Revised total with a note that cladding costs rose, to be detailed at the next stage
options.c: Updated forecast with the increase drawn from contingency, without a change reference
options.d: Increase applied pro rata across all elements to keep the elemental ratios consistent

distractorExplanations.b: A £1.1m movement needs quantified, traceable elemental analysis now, not a note deferred to the next stage.
distractorExplanations.c: Contingency drawdown without a change reference loses the audit trail linking cost movement to the design decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Variances must attach to the causative element (external walls); spreading them distorts the cost plan.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Cost variance reporting ties changes to design decisions with quantified elemental impact. An approval trail should link the change to the client's instruction.

options.a: Preparing NRM2 bills of quantities for call-off tenders, checked by the commercial director
options.b: Leading supply chain negotiations, risk pricing, and margin governance with measured outcomes
options.c: Producing monthly cost value reconciliations for the framework, as reviewed by your manager
options.d: Explaining the NEC4 pricing options and how pain/gain applies under Options C and D

distractorExplanations.a: Measurement checked by others shows Level 2 doing, not Level 3 leading commercial decisions and outcomes.
distractorExplanations.c: Producing CVRs for review is Level 2 application; Level 3 needs advice and leadership with outcomes.
distractorExplanations.d: Explaining contract theory demonstrates Level 1 knowledge, not Level 3 commercial management on live call-offs.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Level 3 commercial management is shown through leadership in pricing, risk, and supply chain outcomes. Ideally across multiple call-offs.

options.a: Traditional elemental cost plan with modular priced as a percentage saving from supplier data
options.b: Modular supplier quotation compared with BCIS traditional £/m² rates for student housing
options.c: Option appraisal with capital cost, programme, factory/offsite assumptions, and risk allowances
options.d: Option appraisal on capital cost only, with programme savings left to the development appraisal

distractorExplanations.a: Supplier-claimed percentage savings are not an option-specific cost model; modular needs its own priced appraisal.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparing a quote with benchmarks is not like-for-like; transport, cranage, interfaces and risk must be added.
distractorExplanations.d: Programme saving (earlier income) is a key modular benefit and belongs in the cost option appraisal.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Modular vs traditional appraisals need option-specific costs including logistics and interfaces. Interface costs between modules and site works should be priced.

options.a: Include VAT at 20% within each elemental rate so the total matches the client's cash outlay
options.b: Exclude VAT from all reports, as VAT is a tax matter for the client's accountants only
options.c: Show VAT at the reduced 5% rate, as JCT IBC works are zero-rated or reduced-rated
options.d: Follow client brief — typically show net construction cost with VAT stated separately

distractorExplanations.a: Rates in UK cost plans are normally net; VAT is stated separately because recovery depends on the client's tax status.
distractorExplanations.b: Clients need VAT treatment stated; non-recoverable VAT is a real project cost and must be visible in reporting.
distractorExplanations.c: VAT rate depends on the type of works, such as new dwellings or conversions, not on the JCT contract form.

options.a: Review scope, risk, efficiencies, and walk-away position; escalate for director approval
options.b: Submit at a loss to secure turnover, planning to recover margin through variations and claims
options.c: Reduce preliminaries and risk allowances to restore margin before submission without director review
options.d: Submit at cost and agree a price increase with the client after award through negotiation

distractorExplanations.b: Bidding at a loss and relying on claims is unsustainable and should be stopped by commercial governance.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting allowances to hit margin mis-prices risk; a negative margin needs review and director escalation.
distractorExplanations.d: Post-award price increases outside the contract mechanism are improper and undermine the tender process.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Pre-submission commercial review includes walk-away analysis and governance on margin. A no-bid decision is a valid outcome.

options.a: Include CIL within NRM1 external works and S106 highway works within substructure
options.b: Identify planning obligations separately from construction cost with timing per planning agreement
options.c: Exclude S106 and CIL from the cost plan, as they are payable only after practical completion
options.d: Carry S106 and CIL within the risk allowance until the planning agreement is signed

distractorExplanations.a: CIL is a charge, not a construction element; planning obligations sit outside NRM1 building works elements.
distractorExplanations.c: CIL is normally due on commencement and S106 triggers vary; both must be timed per the agreements in cash flow.
distractorExplanations.d: Known planning obligations are defined costs, not risks; they should be separately identified, not buried in risk.

options.a: Activity schedule lump sum with payment on completed activities and no target
options.b: Defined cost plus fee with pain/gain share against agreed target at completion
options.c: Defined cost plus fee with no target or share, the contractor carrying no cost risk
options.d: Bill of quantities remeasurement with pain/gain share against the tendered total

distractorExplanations.a: That describes NEC Option A (priced contract with activity schedule), not the Option C target contract.
distractorExplanations.c: That is NEC Option E (cost reimbursable); Option C adds a target with a pain/gain share.
distractorExplanations.d: Remeasurement against a bill is Option B, and a target with a bill is Option D, not Option C.

options.a: Lump sum milestones per the Schedule of Payments, as Red Book works are design-build
options.b: Contractor's monthly statement certified on the Engineer's determination of actual cost plus fee
options.c: Measured works per BOQ and contract valuation procedures in Conditions of Contract
options.d: JCT-style valuation on gross value less 3% retention, applied by the employer's QS

distractorExplanations.a: Red Book is employer-designed and remeasured; schedule-of-payment milestones suit Yellow or Silver Book lump sums.
distractorExplanations.b: Red Book payments are measured BOQ quantities at contract rates, not cost-plus; the Engineer certifies measured value.
distractorExplanations.d: FIDIC uses the Engineer's interim payment certificates and its own retention provisions, not JCT valuation rules.

options.a: Full construction contract on a lump sum, with stage 2 used only for design checks
options.b: Design and build contract on a target cost, fixed before any contractor design input
options.c: Letter of intent for enabling works, with the stage 2 price fixed on first-stage rates
options.d: Pre-construction services agreement with defined prelim design and programme

distractorExplanations.a: Stage 1 does not award the main build contract; the construction price is fixed at stage 2.
distractorExplanations.b: Two-stage engages the contractor early for buildability; the price is not fixed before their stage 1 input.
distractorExplanations.c: Enabling works letters may follow, but stage 1 is a PCSA; the stage 2 price comes from package tendering, not first-stage rates.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Two-stage procurement separates pre-construction engagement from stage 2 price fix. It also defines the scope of stage 2 package competition.

options.a: Contract valuation rules referencing BOQ rates and fair rates hierarchy
options.b: Daywork rates under the RICS definition of prime cost, as BOQ rates are fixed to the original scope
options.c: NEC compensation event assessment based on Defined Cost plus Fee
options.d: A Schedule 2 quotation agreed in advance, which the JCT makes the default valuation route

distractorExplanations.b: Dayworks are the fallback where work cannot be measured; the JCT Valuation Rules start from BOQ rates and pro-rata rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Defined Cost plus Fee is the NEC compensation event method; JCT SBC values variations under its own Valuation Rules.
distractorExplanations.d: A Schedule 2 quotation is an optional route used only when instructed; the default is valuation under the JCT Valuation Rules.

options.a: Agree the cost of compensation events before the Project Manager issues instructions
options.b: Notify and mitigate risk events collaboratively before they become compensation events
options.c: Record contractor delays so delay damages can be deducted at Completion
options.d: Review and accept the contractor's revised programme submitted every four weeks

distractorExplanations.a: Agreeing CE costs is the quotation process; early warnings flag risks before they affect cost, time or quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Early warning is collaborative risk reduction, not a mechanism for building a delay damages case.
distractorExplanations.d: Programme acceptance is a separate clause 31/32 process; early warning meetings deal with notified risks.

options.a: A fresh Find a Tender notice for each call-off above the threshold
options.b: Award to any framework supplier by negotiation once its rates are on the framework list
options.c: Compliance with PCR2015/Procurement Act procedures and framework terms
options.d: Three written quotes under the client's standing orders, as frameworks sit outside PCR2015

distractorExplanations.a: Call-offs from a compliant framework do not need a new advert; the framework procurement already covers that.
distractorExplanations.b: Call-offs must follow the framework's direct award or mini-competition rules; ad hoc negotiation is not compliant.
distractorExplanations.d: Frameworks are regulated by PCR2015/Procurement Act; call-offs follow framework rules, not local quote thresholds.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Public sector framework call-offs must comply with procurement regulations. Call-off follows the framework's mini-competition or direct award terms.

options.a: Contractor designs the whole building to the employer's requirements on a lump sum basis
options.b: Employer design on a large, highly complex project with full bills of quantities and nominated specialists
options.c: Minor works of simple content where the work is valued at around £250k or less, with no named specialists
options.d: Employer design with contractor carrying works risk; moderate complexity without full SBC administration

distractorExplanations.a: Contractor-designed works on ERs suit JCT Design and Build, not the Intermediate Building Contract.
distractorExplanations.b: Large, complex projects with full bills suit JCT SBC; IBC targets moderate complexity without detailed provisions.
distractorExplanations.c: Simple low-value works suit JCT Minor Works; IBC covers moderately complex works, possibly with named specialists.

options.a: Non-compliant — reject or seek cure per tender rules; do not recommend award on price alone
options.b: Award on price, as insurance cover is a post-contract matter checked before start on site
options.c: Add the cost of obtaining insurance to the low bid and re-rank on the adjusted price
options.d: Accept a broker's letter of intent to insure as full compliance with the tender requirements

distractorExplanations.b: Mandatory insurance requirements are pass/fail tender criteria; deferring them to start on site breaches the rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Price adjustment cannot cure a mandatory compliance failure; non-compliant tenders are excluded or cured per rules.
distractorExplanations.d: A letter of intent is not evidence of cover; compliance needs the required insurance in place or a permitted cure.

options.a: Contractor's site diary records of rain days, compared with the average for the month
options.b: Forecast vs actual weather data per contract data with defined compensation thresholds
options.c: Any weather that prevents work on site, valued at Defined Cost for the lost days
options.d: Exceptionally adverse weather as a relevant event, with time but no money under the contract

distractorExplanations.a: NEC uses weather measurements against the 1-in-10-year data in Contract Data, not diary rain days or averages.
distractorExplanations.c: Only weather exceeding the 1-in-10-year return at the stated place is a CE, not any stoppage on site.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the JCT relevant event approach; NEC weather CEs give time and money where thresholds are exceeded.

options.a: Employer, as D&B contractors price only what the ERs state expressly
options.b: The acoustic consultant, since performance gaps are a design team professional indemnity matter
options.c: Contractor if ERs plus applicable law imply performance; clarify via tender query urgently
options.d: Shared equally, as JCT D&B splits risk for matters not covered in the ERs

distractorExplanations.a: D&B contractors carry design responsibility for statutory and functional requirements; silence does not pass risk to the employer.
distractorExplanations.b: The employer's acoustician is not a party to the D&B contract; tender risk sits between employer and contractor.
distractorExplanations.d: JCT D&B has no default 50/50 split; risk follows the ERs, contractor's proposals and statutory requirements.

options.a: Price certainty from fixing the contractor's rates before design is complete
options.b: Early contractor involvement in design, giving buildability input before pricing
options.c: Open competition from any bidder, maximising price competition for the client
options.d: Competitive price with controlled bidder quality and reduced open-market unknowns

distractorExplanations.a: Fixing price before full design is a two-stage or D&B feature, not a benefit of single-stage selective tender.
distractorExplanations.b: Early contractor involvement is the advantage of two-stage tendering; single-stage prices a complete design.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes open tendering; selective tender limits bids to pre-qualified invited contractors.

options.a: Protects a legitimate interest and is not out of all proportion to it
options.b: Is reassessed by the Employer's QS at completion against the actual loss incurred
options.c: Is enforceable only where the employer later proves the actual loss suffered
options.d: Is a weekly percentage of the contract sum, capped at a standard JCT 10% limit

distractorExplanations.b: LDs are agreed in advance in the Contract Particulars; assessing actual loss at completion is general damages, not liquidated damages.
distractorExplanations.c: LDs are recoverable without proving actual loss; that is the purpose of agreeing a liquidated rate.
distractorExplanations.d: JCT sets no standard LD cap; the rate and any cap are entered by the parties in the Contract Particulars.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Since Cavendish v Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67, an LD clause is a penalty only if the detriment is out of all proportion to the employer's legitimate interest in timely completion. A genuine pre-estimate of loss still passes, but it is no longer the test.
mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.prompt: Under a JCT contract, a liquidated damages rate entered in the Contract Particulars will be upheld if it:

options.a: Detailed design and a bill of quantities for remeasurement by the Engineer
options.b: Employer's requirements; contractor designs and executes works to meet them
options.c: Employer's requirements under a turnkey EPC lump sum with most risks on the contractor
options.d: Outline design and a target cost, the contractor paid defined cost plus pain/gain

distractorExplanations.a: Employer design with a remeasured BOQ is the Red Book; the Yellow Book is contractor design to the ERs.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes the Silver Book (EPC/Turnkey); the Yellow Book keeps a more balanced risk allocation.
distractorExplanations.d: Target cost with defined cost is an NEC Option C/D concept, not the FIDIC Yellow Book payment basis.

options.a: Score tender prices and quality submissions to select the preferred contractor
options.b: Agree the contract sum and programme with the preferred bidder ahead of contract award
options.c: Assess financial standing, experience, H&S, and capacity before inviting tender
options.d: Set the employer's pre-tender estimate and cash flow forecast for the project budget

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses PQQ shortlisting with the later tender evaluation stage, where price and quality submissions are scored.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes post-tender negotiation with the preferred bidder, which happens after tenders are returned, not at PQQ.
distractorExplanations.d: The pre-tender estimate is the client QS's cost planning task; the PQQ assesses bidders, not the budget.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: A pre-qualification questionnaire (now a selection questionnaire, or conditions of participation under the Procurement Act 2023) screens bidders on financial standing, relevant experience, health and safety record and capacity before any tender is issued. Only firms that pass are invited to tender, so the later price/quality evaluation compares capable contractors rather than filtering out unsuitable ones.

options.a: Fully designed schemes priced as a lump sum against the contractor's activity schedule
options.b: Fully measured works where a bill of quantities is remeasured at the tendered rates
options.c: Projects with an agreed target where overruns and savings are shared by formula
options.d: High uncertainty scopes needing open-book defined cost with fee control

distractorExplanations.a: That describes NEC4 Option A (priced contract with activity schedule), suited to well-defined designs.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes NEC4 Option B (priced contract with bill of quantities), not cost reimbursable Option E.
distractorExplanations.c: Pain/gain share against a target is NEC4 Option C/D; Option E pays defined cost plus fee with no target.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: NEC Option E fits uncertain scope with open-book cost reimbursement; the client carries cost risk and controls it through the fee and defined cost rules.

options.a: Submit compliant tender query requesting priority and clarification before submission
options.b: Price the drawings, as they take precedence over the ERs under the usual order of documents
options.c: Price the cheaper reading and rely on a post-award change to recover any later shortfall
options.d: Qualify the bid stating the cheaper reading was priced, and submit it unaltered

distractorExplanations.b: There is no general rule that drawings beat ERs; document priority is contract-specific and must be clarified.
distractorExplanations.c: Pricing a hidden low interpretation distorts tender comparison and shifts the dispute to post-award.
distractorExplanations.d: A qualification may make the bid non-compliant; the query process exists to resolve the conflict first.

options.a: A single payment certificate at practical completion, with deductions agreed at final account
options.b: Specified notices within statutory/contractual deadlines showing sums due and deductions
options.c: Notices issued only once a dispute is referred to adjudication, setting out the sum claimed
options.d: A pay less notice served at any point up to the final date for payment, stating sums withheld

distractorExplanations.a: JCT and the Construction Act require interim payment notices each cycle, not one certificate at completion.
distractorExplanations.c: Payment and pay less notices are part of every payment cycle, not a step triggered by adjudication.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong timing: a JCT pay less notice must be given no later than 5 days before the final date for payment.

options.a: Comply, then submit a variation claim with the final account under JCT valuation rules
options.b: Refuse to act until the Project Manager issues a priced quotation for the changed Scope
options.c: Comply and give an early warning only, as Scope changes are valued at the final account
options.d: Comply and notify compensation event if not own fault within NEC timescales

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses NEC compensation events with JCT variations valued at final account; NEC assesses CEs as they arise.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong party: under NEC the Contractor submits quotations; it must comply with PM instructions meanwhile.
distractorExplanations.c: An early warning is not a CE notification; NEC changes are assessed via quotations, not at final account.

options.a: Percentage withheld from interim payments released at practical completion and defects period end
options.b: A performance bond of 10% of contract value lodged by the contractor before site possession
options.c: A deduction from the final account equal to liquidated damages for late completion of works
options.d: Percentage withheld from interim payments, released in one sum only after the final certificate

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses retention with a performance bond, which is third-party security, not a payment deduction.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses retention with liquidated damages, which compensate for delay rather than secure defects.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong timing: JCT releases half the retention at practical completion and the rest at end of rectification period.

options.a: Competitive quotes from three local firms under the authority's below-threshold standing orders
options.b: Structured advertised procedure with defined evaluation criteria and standstill
options.c: Publish a contract award notice after signing, with no tender notice or standstill period
options.d: Advertised procedure with evaluation criteria agreed with bidders after tenders are opened

distractorExplanations.a: Three-quote standing orders apply below threshold; above threshold the statutory advertised regime applies.
distractorExplanations.c: Skips the tender notice and standstill that above-threshold procedures require before contract signature.
distractorExplanations.d: Evaluation criteria must be published before bids are received; setting them after opening breaches transparency.

options.a: Suits large multi-phase schemes needing sectional completion and full contractor design
options.b: Requires a full bill of quantities and named specialists as the main pricing documents
options.c: Simpler administration for low-risk small works — not for complex major projects
options.d: Includes detailed fluctuation and named subcontractor clauses for big projects

distractorExplanations.a: Sectional completion and full contractor design point to SBC or Design and Build, not Minor Works.
distractorExplanations.b: Minor Works is priced on drawings, specification or work schedules; quantities suit SBC With Quantities.
distractorExplanations.d: Minor Works deliberately omits detailed fluctuation and named subcontractor machinery to stay simple.

options.a: Accepted as standard, since unforeseen ground risk sits with the employer under JCT forms
options.b: Priced by the QS as a provisional sum and added to the bid without seeking clarification
options.c: Treated as a tiebreaker in favour of the bidder, as it shows realistic ground risk pricing
options.d: Evaluated — may be non-compliant if tender required unconditional acceptance of site info

distractorExplanations.a: JCT SBC leaves unforeseen ground risk with the contractor by default, so the qualification shifts risk.
distractorExplanations.b: The QS cannot price a bidder's qualification away; it must be clarified, withdrawn or assessed for compliance.
distractorExplanations.c: Qualifications are tested for compliance and risk, not rewarded as an evaluation tiebreaker.

options.a: Early dispute avoidance and binding adjudication decisions per FIDIC procedure
options.b: Final and binding arbitration of disputes with no route to challenge the board's award
options.c: Certifying interim payments and determining claims as the Engineer under Sub-Clause 3.7
options.d: Mediating disputes after completion, issuing non-binding recommendations to the parties

distractorExplanations.b: DAAB decisions are binding but not final; a party can give notice of dissatisfaction and go to arbitration.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the DAAB with the Engineer, who makes determinations under Sub-Clause 3.7.
distractorExplanations.d: The DAAB is a standing board from the start of the works and its decisions are binding, not mediation.

options.a: A shortlist limited to pre-qualified bidders, reducing evaluation time and bid volume
options.b: Wide bidder pool with higher bid review burden and potential non-compliant low bids
options.c: Direct negotiation with one preferred contractor on price before any formal tender
options.d: Higher prices than restricted tender, because fewer contractors can submit a bid

distractorExplanations.a: Describes the restricted procedure, where a PQQ shortlist limits bid numbers; open tender has no shortlist.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes negotiated single-source procurement, the opposite of an open competitive tender.
distractorExplanations.d: Open tender lets any contractor bid, so it widens competition rather than reducing the field.

options.a: The main pricing options A to F that set how the contractor is paid for the works
options.b: Z clauses drafted by the client to amend core clauses for project-specific risks
options.c: Additional conditions such as delay damages, performance bonds, and sectional completion
options.d: The core clauses 1 to 9 setting general obligations, time, quality and payment

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses main Options A–F (payment mechanism) with the X secondary options added on top.
distractorExplanations.b: Z clauses are bespoke additional conditions; X clauses are the standard published secondary options.
distractorExplanations.d: Core clauses apply to every NEC contract; X clauses are optional additions to them.

options.a: Termination by the contractor for repudiatory breach as soon as possession is a day late
options.b: Liquidated damages payable by the employer at the rate stated in the Contract Particulars
options.c: Extension of time only, as late possession is a neutral event carrying no loss and expense
options.d: Extension of time and/or loss and expense per contract if employer delay is relevant event

distractorExplanations.a: Short delay in possession is a relevant event and matter, not an immediate repudiatory termination right.
distractorExplanations.b: Liquidated damages run from contractor to employer for late completion, not the other way.
distractorExplanations.c: Late possession is an employer default: it is both a relevant event (time) and a relevant matter (money).

options.a: Price and quality criteria weighted per published methodology
options.b: Lowest compliant price, with quality used as a pass/fail minimum standard
options.c: Quality scores first, with price opened after the preferred bidder is chosen
options.d: Price and quality weighted by criteria the panel sets after reviewing bids received

distractorExplanations.b: Describes lowest-price award with a quality gate, not a weighted best value (MEAT) evaluation of price and quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Best value combines price and quality in one weighted score; opening price after selection is quality-based selection.
distractorExplanations.d: Weightings must be published before bids arrive; setting them after review breaches transparency.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: Public best value procurement uses weighted price/quality evaluation, not price alone.

options.a: Pricing the works only, with design responsibility left with the employer's architect
options.b: Developing employer's requirements to deliver compliant completed works
options.c: Checking the architect's design for buildability while the employer keeps design liability
options.d: Completing design with a fitness-for-purpose duty, the JCT Design and Build default

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a traditional build-only contract; under JCT DB the contractor completes the design.
distractorExplanations.c: Buildability review is a PCSA or ECI service; JCT DB puts design completion and liability on the contractor.
distractorExplanations.d: The JCT DB default design duty is reasonable skill and care, not fitness for purpose.

options.a: Full construction works to start on site under the PCSA while the contract sum is agreed
options.b: Award of the main contract without competition once the PCSA is signed by both parties
options.c: Early contractor involvement for design development, programming, and tender pricing inputs
options.d: Transfer of design liability for the concept design from the architect to the contractor

distractorExplanations.a: A PCSA covers pre-construction services; main works need the construction contract (or a limited LOI).
distractorExplanations.b: A PCSA does not itself award the main contract; award depends on the procurement strategy and agreed price.
distractorExplanations.d: Design liability passes via novation and the D&B contract, not through the PCSA.

options.a: Scoring quality first and inviting the highest-scoring quality bidder to submit its price
options.b: Ranking bids by price, then using quality scores to break ties between equal-priced bidders
options.c: Adjusting sub-criteria weightings after opening to reflect the strongest submissions
options.d: Documented scoring of quality sub-criteria and arithmetically combined weighted result

distractorExplanations.a: That is quality-based selection; a 60/40 matrix combines both price and quality scores for every compliant bidder.
distractorExplanations.b: Using quality as a tiebreaker ignores the published 40% quality weighting, which must be scored and combined for every bid.
distractorExplanations.c: Weightings and sub-criteria are fixed pre-tender; changing them after opening breaches equal treatment.

options.a: Projected defined cost of event with disallowable cost rules
options.b: Bill rates for similar work, adjusted for changed conditions
options.c: Daywork rates for labour, plant and materials per JCT schedule
options.d: Fair valuation of delay days by the Project Manager on completion

distractorExplanations.b: Valuing at bill rates is the JCT valuation rules approach, not NEC Clause 63 defined cost assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Daywork schedules belong to JCT valuation; NEC uses defined cost plus fee via its Schedule of Cost Components.
distractorExplanations.d: NEC assesses CEs at the time by forecast defined cost and programme effect, not a fair valuation at completion.

options.a: Transfer of all building design to the contractor, as under JCT Design and Build
options.b: Identification of CDP works in contract documents with appropriate design liability insurance
options.c: A fitness-for-purpose design duty on the contractor for CDP works as the JCT default
options.d: Novation of the architect to the contractor so the CDP design team sits under one contract

distractorExplanations.a: CDP covers only identified portions of design; whole-building design transfer is JCT Design and Build.
distractorExplanations.c: The JCT SBC CDP default is the same skill and care as an architect, not fitness for purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: Novation is a Design and Build practice; CDP works are identified within an otherwise employer-designed scheme.

options.a: Hold original framework rates fixed for the full term, with inflation absorbed by suppliers
options.b: Re-tender the whole framework via a new Find a Tender notice before any further call-off
options.c: Follow framework rules — mini-competition or indexation/rebenchmark per terms
options.d: Let suppliers resubmit rates unilaterally, with the client accepting the revised schedule

distractorExplanations.a: Most frameworks include indexation or rebenchmarking; holding rates ignores the agreed refresh mechanism.
distractorExplanations.b: A live framework continues under its own call-off rules; a full re-procurement is not needed for a refresh.
distractorExplanations.d: Rate changes follow the framework's agreed procedure, not unilateral supplier resubmission.

options.a: Retention, liquidated damages and insurance, which together act as the contractor's bonds
options.b: Professional indemnity and contract works insurance cover taken out by the employer
options.c: Advance payment bonds, as performance security is rare on UK building contracts
options.d: Bid bonds, performance bonds, and parent company guarantees per contract risk profile

distractorExplanations.a: Retention and LDs are contract mechanisms, not bonds; bonds are third-party financial guarantees.
distractorExplanations.b: PI and contract works insurance cover loss events; they are not third-party security guaranteeing the contractor's performance.
distractorExplanations.c: Performance bonds and parent company guarantees are common UK security; advance payment bonds are used when an advance is paid.

options.a: Material/labour price movement via formula indices during contract period
options.b: Variations to scope instructed by the architect and valued at bill rates
options.c: Currency exchange movements on imported materials, recovered as loss and expense
options.d: Tender inflation from estimate date to tender, added to the cost plan by the QS

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses fluctuations (input price movement) with variations (scope changes valued under the valuation rules).
distractorExplanations.c: Loss and expense compensates relevant matters; fluctuations use contribution or formula options, not L&E.
distractorExplanations.d: Pre-tender inflation is a cost plan allowance; JCT fluctuations cover price movement after the base date.

options.a: Award to the lowest priced bidder once the portal closes and bids are opened
options.b: Audit trail, deadline enforcement, and equal information to all bidders
options.c: Bidders can view competitors' prices once the bids open, for transparency
options.d: Clarification answers are sent only to the bidder who raised the question

distractorExplanations.a: The portal manages submissions; award still follows the published price/quality evaluation.
distractorExplanations.c: Competitors' prices stay confidential; transparency means equal process, not sharing commercial bids.
distractorExplanations.d: Clarification responses go to all bidders (anonymised) so every bidder has equal information.

options.a: A two-stage price where the stage two price is fixed as a lump sum under Option A
options.b: Design and build risk transfer with the contractor's price fixed at stage one tender
options.c: Collaborative design development with target cost evolution before main construction
options.d: Partnering between several contractors on a multi-party programme of linked projects

distractorExplanations.a: X22 is used only with Options C and E; a stage two lump sum under Option A is not an X22 route.
distractorExplanations.b: X22 develops the price during stage one; fixing it at the stage one tender defeats early involvement.
distractorExplanations.d: Multi-party partnering across linked projects is Option X12, not X22 early contractor involvement.

mrics-quantity-surveying-readiness-check.explanation: NEC Option X22 (Early Contractor Involvement) is used with main Options C or E and splits the work into Stage One, where the contractor helps develop the design, programme and price with the client's team, and Stage Two construction, which proceeds only when the Project Manager instructs it. The target is built up during Stage One and a budget incentive rewards savings, so X22 supports collaborative design and target cost development rather than an early fixed price.

options.a: Binding full JCT terms from issue, so the employer carries no added risk until signing
options.b: Liability for the contractor's full tender sum even where the LOI caps spend lower
options.c: Exposure to the contractor's overheads only, as LOIs cannot authorise physical works
options.d: Limited scope, unclear terms, and payment/dispute exposure if full contract delayed

distractorExplanations.a: An LOI does not import the full JCT terms; its limited scope and terms are the source of employer risk.
distractorExplanations.b: A properly drafted LOI spend cap limits the employer's liability; it does not trigger the full tender sum.
distractorExplanations.c: LOIs often authorise early works on site; exposure covers those works, not just overheads.

options.a: Relevant event, causal delay to completion, and notice within contractual period
options.b: Rain on any working day recorded in site diaries, without comparison to historic data
